headline: CEDAR IS
*ROT-PROOF?*
beats.vo: Is cedar *rot-proof*? Not quite. It resists rot, and here's how to make it last.

headline: KEEP CEDAR
*OFF THE DIRT*
beats.vo: Keep the boards *off the dirt*. A treated *kickboard* takes the ground moisture and is easy to replace.
beats.note: band at 1.3x on the 0.675 cover scale (0.88x effective), panned 135-155 px left so the barrel, wheelbarrow and pots at the left edge of the photo are out of frame; the ring sits on the kickboard

headline: CUT ENDS DRINK
*11X FASTER*
beats.vo: *Cut ends* soak up water about *eleven times faster*, so post tops get *caps*.

headline: BLACK STREAKS?
CHECK THE *NAILS*
beats.vo: *Black streaks* at the nails? That's the wrong *fasteners* reacting with the cedar. Use *stainless* or *hot-dip galvanized*.

beats.label: DRY WOOD. DRY DAY.
headline: DON'T WAIT
TO *STAIN*
beats.vo: Built a fence this fall? Don't leave it bare all winter. Once it's *dry*, *stain* it within a couple of weeks, on a dry day.

post.caption: Cedar fences in the Lower Mainland resist rot, but cedar isn't rot-proof. Keep the boards off the soil with a kickboard, cap the posts (cut ends soak up water about 11x faster), use stainless or hot-dip galvanized fasteners, and stain new cedar within a couple of weeks once it's dry, on a dry day that meets the stain label's temperature.
post.alt: A new framed cedar fence, close-ups of a kickboard, post caps and overlapping boards, and an orange-stained cedar fence.
